description: Why Britain went to war in South Africa, scorched earth and what it did to Britain.
content_html:
Britain and South Africa in 1899

By the late 1890s, southern Africa had become one of the most contested regions on earth. The discovery of gold in the Transvaal in 1886 transformed what had been a farming republic into the richest territory on the continent. British mine owners and financiers, led by figures such as Cecil Rhodes, pressed the British government to extend its control over Boer-run territories. The Boers — descendants of Dutch settlers — fiercely resisted British domination. Diplomatic negotiations broke down, and on 11 October 1899 the Boers declared war and immediately invaded British-held Natal and the Cape Colony.

Key Fact

Gold was discovered in the Transvaal in 1886. British desire to control this wealth was a leading cause of the Second Boer War, which began in October 1899.

Early Boer Success and the Sieges

The opening months of the war shocked the British public. Well-armed Boer commandos using guerrilla tactics — small, mobile fighting units that knew the terrain — inflicted a series of embarrassing defeats on British forces during “Black Week” in December 1899. Three major British garrisons at Ladysmith, Mafeking and Kimberley were surrounded and besieged. Britain had badly underestimated its enemy.

The relief of Mafeking in May 1900 triggered wild celebrations across Britain. Colonel Robert Baden-Powell had held the town for 217 days. The exuberant public response — crowds filled the streets and a new word, “mafficking,” entered the language to describe rowdy celebrating — showed how deeply the war had gripped the public imagination. However, the easy victories that many had predicted never came.

The Boers were experienced farmers who knew the South African landscape intimately. They were skilled horsemen and marksmen, equipped with modern Mauser rifles. Their guerrilla tactics meant they could strike British supply lines and retreat before the much larger British army could respond. British commanders, trained for conventional set-piece battles in Europe, were slow to adapt.

When Field Marshal Lord Roberts and General Kitchener arrived in early 1900, they rapidly reversed the early setbacks. British forces captured Pretoria, the Transvaal capital, in June 1900. However, rather than surrendering, the Boer commandos dispersed into the countryside and began a prolonged guerrilla campaign.

Scorched Earth and Concentration Camps

To defeat the guerrilla campaign, Kitchener introduced a strategy of systematic devastation. British forces burned Boer farms, destroyed crops and livestock, and rounded up Boer civilians — mainly women and children — into concentration camps. The intention was to deny the commandos food and support. By 1902 approximately 154,000 Boer civilians were held in these camps.

The conditions were appalling. Overcrowding, inadequate food, poor sanitation and disease — especially measles and typhoid — killed approximately 26,000 Boer civilians, most of them children. Black Africans were held in separate camps where death rates were at least as high; around 20,000 died there. These figures remain controversial but represent the consensus of modern scholarship.

Key Fact

Emily Hobhouse, a British welfare campaigner, visited the camps in 1901 and published a detailed report exposing the death rates and suffering. Her findings caused a public outcry in Britain and changed the tone of debate about the war.

Emily Hobhouse travelled to the camps in early 1901, gathering evidence on food rations, medical provision and mortality. Her report was met with hostility from the government. The War Secretary, St John Brodrick, dismissed her findings and initially barred her return to South Africa. Under public pressure, a commission chaired by Millicent Fawcett was sent to investigate. The Fawcett Commission broadly confirmed Hobhouse’s findings and recommended improvements; conditions improved significantly after 1901, though deaths continued until the war ended in 1902.

Changing Attitudes in Britain

The war exposed deep divisions within British society. Supporters, known as “jingoes” or “khaki imperialists,” celebrated the war as a defence of British interests and empire. The 1900 general election was called early to exploit war enthusiasm; it became known as the Khaki Election because the Conservatives under Lord Salisbury used patriotic feeling to win a comfortable majority.

However, a growing “pro-Boer” movement, which included Liberal politicians such as David Lloyd George and campaigners such as Emily Hobhouse, condemned the war as immoral and imperialist. Lloyd George faced hostile crowds when he spoke out at public meetings. The camps controversy converted many moderates to criticism of the war. By 1901–1902, even some supporters acknowledged that the methods used had damaged Britain’s moral reputation abroad.

The Treaty of Vereeniging, signed in May 1902, ended the war. The Boer republics were absorbed into the British Empire but were promised eventual self-government; that promise was fulfilled in 1910 with the creation of the Union of South Africa. The war had cost approximately £220 million and around 22,000 British soldiers’ lives, mostly to disease. It left Britain isolated diplomatically and damaged the image of empire at home and abroad.
exam_tip_html: For a ‘5 marks — Source Utility’ question, never say a source is useless because it is biased. Instead, explain what its content tells you and use your own contextual knowledge to assess how far that information is useful for the specific enquiry. For 8-mark ‘Explain Significance’ questions on the Boer War, you must address significance at the time (e.g. effect on British public opinion) AND significance over time (e.g. how the camps debate fed into Liberal reform debates).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Second Boer War (1899–1902) began over control of gold-rich South Africa. Early Boer guerrilla tactics humiliated Britain before Kitchener’s scorched-earth strategy turned the tide.
  • Concentration camps for Boer and Black African civilians caused the deaths of tens of thousands, largely through disease. Emily Hobhouse’s 1901 report and the Fawcett Commission exposed the scandal.
  • The war created a “khaki” wave of imperial support but also a significant “pro-Boer” movement. By 1902 it had shaken British confidence in empire and fuelled the social reform debates of the Edwardian era.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Boers' military tactics in the early phase of the Second Boer War.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks for a developed point. Example: The Boers used guerrilla tactics (1), attacking British supply lines with small mobile commando units before retreating into the countryside (1). Mastering: accurate feature with precise supporting detail. Developing: feature stated but not developed.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the British concentration camps set up during the Boer War.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for supporting detail). Feature 1 examples: overcrowding; inadequate food rations; poor sanitation; high disease rates (measles, typhoid). Feature 2 examples: held mainly women and children; approximately 26,000 Boer civilian deaths; Black Africans held in separate camps. Mastering: two precise features, each with accurate supporting detail. Secure: two features with some supporting detail. Developing: one or two features, limited detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the Second Boer War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Developed explanation of one cause linked to outcome, supported by accurate contextual knowledge. E.g. the discovery of gold in the Transvaal in 1886 made the republic hugely valuable; British mine owners and financiers pressed the government to extend control; Boer resistance to British domination led to diplomatic breakdown and war in October 1899. Secure (3–4): Clear cause with some development. Developing (1–2): Simple identification with limited development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Emily Hobhouse's 1901 report on the concentration camps.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Developed consequence with precise supporting knowledge. E.g. Hobhouse's report triggered a public outcry that divided opinion in Britain; the government responded by commissioning the Fawcett Commission, which broadly confirmed her findings and recommended improvements; the pro-Boer movement grew, with Liberal politicians like Lloyd George using the scandal to attack the government's conduct of the war. Secure (3–4): Clear consequence with some development. Developing (1–2): Simple statement of a consequence.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Boer War for attitudes to the British Empire.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): Significance at the time AND over time, both substantiated. At the time: the Khaki Election showed public support; concentration camps created the first widespread anti-imperial movement; Emily Hobhouse's revelations damaged the moral image of empire. Over time: the war raised questions about whether military force alone could maintain empire; it contributed to the reform debates of the Liberal government after 1906; influenced later critiques of empire and independence movements. Secure (5–6): Significance at the time and over time, with some development of each. Developing (3–4): Significance mainly at the time, or over time, not both. Emerging (1–2): Simple assertion.

practice_questions.text: 'The concentration camps were the most significant consequence of the Second Boer War for Britain.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Agrees and disagrees using own contextual knowledge, reaches substantiated overall judgement. Agree: camps caused massive civilian deaths; Hobhouse's report created a humanitarian crisis debate; Fawcett Commission forced policy change; 'pro-Boer' movement fed into Liberal reform thinking. Disagree: military cost (~22,000 British lives) and financial cost (~£220 million) were also transformative; diplomatic isolation (Splendid Isolation) had wider consequences; Khaki Election showed pro-empire sentiment remained strong. Secure (7–9): Clear agreement and disagreement, some development, some conclusion. Developing (4–6): Mainly one-sided with limited development. Emerging (1–3): Simple agreement or disagreement only.

glossary_terms.definition: The Afrikaner-ruled republic in southern Africa where gold was discovered in 1886, a central cause of the Second Boer War.
A town in Natal besieged by Boer forces from November 1899 until its relief in February 1900.
Hit-and-run warfare in which small, mobile units strike quickly and then withdraw, avoiding pitched battles.
Enclosed camps set up by the British to hold Boer civilians during the guerrilla phase of the war; poor conditions led to mass deaths.
British supporters of aggressive imperial policy; the term was applied to those who enthusiastically backed the Boer War.
